facts.claim: Full title: Bounce: Mozart, Federer, Picasso, Beckham and the Science of Success (Matthew Syed, 2010). Its central point is the primacy of practice over innate talent.
Syed engages Gladwell's 10,000-hour idea and Anders Ericsson's research: excellence generally takes around ten years or 10,000 hours of purposeful practice, often with coaching.

In the study of violin students the top performers averaged about 10,000 hours of serious practice, the least skilled about 4,000; practice time was the only factor directly linked to achievement. (Another source gives the middle group 8,000 and lowest 6,000; figures vary.)
Purposeful practice means pushing past your comfort zone; people tend to stop practising purposefully once they reach a comfortable level, top performers keep going beyond their current skills.
Ericsson calls the visible moment of brilliance 'the iceberg illusion': years of unseen practice lie beneath it.
Syed grew up on an unremarkable road in south-east England with no sporting background; he became England's top table tennis player and a two-time Olympian.
For a period in the 1980s his street and the surrounding area produced more outstanding table tennis players than the rest of the nation combined.

A teacher at his local school, who was England's top table tennis coach (named Peter Charters in summaries), recruited Syed, his older brother and other promising children to a local club (Omega) with 24-hour access.
The brothers practised against each other for hours a day, starting on a tournament-sized table in their parents' large garage.
Syed concedes that if more young people had shared his opportunities he might not have been number one in England, possibly 'number one thousand and one'.
At the 2000 Sydney Olympics Syed was 'humiliated', playing far below his best at his most important tournament.

Syed explains choking with two brain systems, explicit and implicit. Under pressure control of a familiar task shifts to the explicit system, which 'cannot do many things at once', and the expert struggles with what they had mastered. Example: carrying a full glass of wine across an expensive carpet makes you slow down and watch each step.
Andre Agassi's father reasoned that a child who hit 2,500 balls a day would be unbeatable (Syed's example of volume).
Syed accepts that the rules do not apply directly to less complex sports such as running.

Later research tempers the practice thesis: a 2014 meta-analysis by Macnamara, Hambrick and Oswald found deliberate practice explained about 26% of performance differences in games, 21% in music, 18% in sports.
facts.source: Macnamara et al. 2014 (Psychological Science); also used in approved story 1426

facts.claim: Syed attributes Roger Federer's ability to anticipate serves to learned, practised skill rather than faster reactions.

One summary describes the Omega club as a small, one-table hut open around the clock for members only, where Syed trained with his brother; Peter Charters, a teacher at the local primary school and table tennis enthusiast, invited interested children there.

Syed describes novices as consciously monitoring what they do while they build the neural framework for a task; under pressure the explicit system pulls a skilled player back toward beginner-style play and disrupts the smooth workings of the subconscious.
facts.source: interview excerpt and search summaries of Bounce

facts.claim: Reviewer Mick Hume notes that Syed concludes choking 'just happens' with nothing to be done, and argues this explanation risks sounding as biologically determinist as the talent myths Syed rejects.
A summary says the book recounts severely injured soldiers injected with saline whose pain subsided while they believed it was morphine (a placebo example of mind affecting body).
A summary says that before big competitions Syed puts things in perspective by thinking about relationships, health and family, which reduces the pressure.
